Summary -PFSs considered in this study

In sum, the ppp-based PFSs that we will use in our two simulation studies are the ppp GM , ppp S , ppp RB , and ppp SM. Berkhof et al. (2004) further proposed another ppp approach, this one based on centering the discrepancy measure around its conditional expectation given θ. While this approach may be of interest for non-centered discrepancy measures, for the current paper for which T = l * z this centering has no effect since E[l * z |θ] = 0 by construction (Snijders, 2001). This new approach effectively reduces to ppp GM . We therefore do not consider this alternative ppp further; see Berkhof et al. (2004) for more details. We proceed to explain the details of each simulation study.

Methods

We conducted two separate simulation studies to compare the relative performance of the ppp-based person-fit approaches using l * z as the discrepancy measure. The first simulation study is entirely based on model-fitting response patterns. This simulation serves three purposes: (1) to assess the empirical Type I error rates for each person-fit strategy at the nominal 5% significance level, (2) to derive empirically calibrated 5% thresholds for each person-fit approach to use in aberrant response detection (in the second simulation study), and (3) to compare the performance of the four ppp-based person-fit strategies (ppp GM , ppp S , ppp RB , ppp SM ) under the null model of no aberrant response behavior.

We will refer to this simulation as the 'Type I Error study'. Next, we conducted a second simulation study aimed at assessing the performance of the various approaches in detecting three different types of aberrant response behavior: lack of motivation, item disclosure, and speeding. Our simulation study followed the same set-up of previous research by De La Torre and Deng (2008) and Sinharay (2015a). For each type of aberrant response behavior, all N persons in a generated dataset exhibited that particular answering behavior. The item parameters of each replication, and the calibrated thresholds (averaged across replications) derived from the Type I Error study, were re-used in the corresponding replication of the power studies and were thus unaffected by the imputation of aberrant behavior into the generated data. We will refer to the ensemble of these three simulations as the 'Power studies'. Below we explain the general set-up of each simulation. All the R scripts and output files of the two simulation studies are openly available at https://osf.io/rsfv7/overview?view_only=0eda2c21f6f2476db10cb128188c23cc.

Observe that two types of PFS thresholds used for flagging aberrant response patterns are considered in the Type I Error study. A nominal threshold of a PFS is based on known or idealized distributional properties, when available. For example, the l * z PFS is asymptotically standard normally distributed (Snijders, 2001), thus -1.64 (the 5% quantile) is routinely used as the 5% nominal threshold. As for the ppp's, although they are probabilities (thus constrained to [0, 1]), they lack a known reference distribution (Bayarri & Berger, 2000; Robins et al., 2000). We tentatively used 0.05 as the 5% nominal threshold for a ppp, but this choice requires validation. This relates to the second purpose of the Type I Error study, namely, to check whether such nominal thresholds hold in practice. To this end, calibrated PFS thresholds that are empirically validated by the data were derived and used for comparison. A calibrated threshold is a quantile of the distribution of PFS values found by generating a large number of model-fitting response vectors and computing the PFS for each vector. This procedure is prior predictive in nature because it only depends on the prior distribution used to generate the model parameters (in our case, the θ parameters); observed data are not taken into account for threshold calibration. We used a uniform distribution as the reference prior for θ to estimate the calibrated thresholds because that ensured we had enough response vectors at every ability level considered. This allowed us to study Type I error rates and power not only on average (i.e., for calibrated thresholds that are averaged over θ) as is commonly done in practice, but also conditionally on the ability level θ.

In practice, the procedure that we advocate for a ppp-based person-fit analysis consists of two steps. In the calibration step, a large number of model-fitting response vectors is generated from the (fitted or known) IRT model, with θ drawn from a chosen reference distribution. The PFS is computed for each response vector and its quantile (for instance, at 5%) is saved as the threshold. In the implementation step, the PFS is computed for each examinee in the observed data set of interest. Response patterns with a PFS value below the threshold are flagged as not conforming to the model (they are 'aberrant'). This is the procedure that we followed in the simulation studies, described next; the empirical example that follows illustrates both steps with real data.

Type I Error study

The Type I Error study included a single factor, test length (I = 12, 30, 60). The sample size was fixed at N = 1000 because, with known item parameters and a fixed prior for θ, the posterior of the nth examinee's ability θ n depends only on their response vector y n . Data were generated under the 2PL (Equation 1), with the discrimination parameters sampled from the Uniform(1.1, 2.5) distribution and the difficulty parameters sampled from the N (0, 1) distribution. Each test length condition was replicated 100 times, to account for sampling variability. In each replication a new set of item parameters was generated. The true ability parameters of the N = 1000 persons were generated by splitting the interval [-3, 3] into ten bins of equal width and drawing 100 abilities uniformly within each bin.

The posterior distribution of θ was approximated via a grid method. Specifically, for each person, a thin grid of equally spaced candidate θ values from -6 to 6 in steps of 0.01 was considered. The unnormalized log-posterior log p(θ|y) ∝ log p(y|θ) + log p(θ) was computed at each grid point, with a standard normal distribution prior placed on θ. S = 250 θ values from the grid were sampled, with replacement, with probability proportional to the normalized discrete posterior distribution p(θ|y). Preliminary simulations confirmed that 250 samples were sufficient for a stable estimation of the ppp values.

For each condition and replication, the four person-fit strategies were applied (ppp GM , ppp S , ppp RB , ppp SM ). The classical l * z was also computed for comparison purposes only, using the maximum likelihood estimate of θ in the computations. Our main goal is to compare the performance of the four ppp statistics. The proportion of persons flagged at the nominal 5% threshold was recorded for each approach. Additionally, the empirical 5th percentile of each statistic's distribution was computed per replication and then averaged across replications within each test length condition. This yielded calibrated 5% critical thresholds, to be used in the three power studies. Using these thresholds, we also recorded the proportion of persons flagged separately for each ability bin. For completeness, we also considered critical levels other than 5%, namely, 1%, 2%, and 10%. The results were largely consistent with the 5% level. We defer results based on these critical levels to the supplementary material.

Power studies

The general setup of each power simulation was the same as what we described above for the Type I Error study. The only main difference is that, after having generated each model-fitting data set, we modified the response probabilities of each person to reflect each of the three aberrant response behaviors (lack of motivation, item disclosure, and speeding). In doing so, we introduced an additional simulation factor for two of the three misfit types, namely the proportion of aberrant behavior-induced item scores (factor 'PropAbIt'), as described below.

Lack of motivation was operationalized by replacing the correct response probability implied by the 2PL model with the fixed value of .20 for the easiest fraction of items (Glas & Meijer, 2003). The 'easiness' of the items was indicated by the difficulty parameters β i (lower = easier). The proportion of affected items, which we refer to as PropAbIt, is a factor with three levels (PropAbIt = 1/6, 1/3, 1/2). This yielded a fully crossed 3(I) × 3(PropAbIt) design with 9 conditions, 100 replications each. Item disclosure was operationalized by setting the response probability to 1 for the most difficult fraction of items (De La Torre & Deng, 2008; Sinharay, 2015a). Similarly to the lack of motivation simulation, the proportion of affected items was manipulated in the exact same way (PropAbIt = 1/6, 1/3, 1/2), yielding 9 conditions in total. Finally, speeding was operationalized by setting the response probability to .20 for the most difficult one-third of the items (Sinharay, 2015a). This yielded 3 conditions in total for this study (one per test length).

For each condition and replication across all three power studies, detection rates were computed at the empirically calibrated 5% thresholds derived from the Type I Error study. The primary outcome of interest was the proportion of persons correctly flagged as misfitting (i.e., power), compared across the four ppp statistics and across levels of I and the proportion of aberrant items where applicable. Detection rates were also recorded separately for each ability bin, as in the Type I Error study, and we also considered the 1%, 2%, and 10% critical levels (see the supplementary material). The classical l * z was also computed simply as a well-known term of reference.

Results

Simulation Study 1: Type I Error

Figure 1 displays the empirical Type I error rates at the nominal 5% thresholds, averaged across the 100 replications (see Figure S1 in the supplementary materials for the error rates at other critical levels). The classical l * z was well calibrated, consistently flagging between 4.6% and 5.5% of model-fitting response patterns. Among the ppp approaches, ppp S (mean Type I error rates between 4.5% and 5.2%) was well calibrated. The ppp SM statistic was slightly conservative (between 3.9% and 4.2%). In contrast, ppp GM and ppp RB were conservative, with empirical Type I error rates ranging between 1.8% and 2.0% (ppp GM ) and between 1.7% and 2.0% (ppp RB ). The results were largely stable across the test length factor I. The observed deviations from the 5% nominal error rate motivate the use of empirically calibrated thresholds, as described next. Figure 2 shows the empirically calibrated 5% detection thresholds for the ppp PFSs, averaged across replications (see Figure S2 in the supplementary materials for the calibrated thresholds at other critical levels). The plot does not display the results for the classical l * z because its threshold lives on the standard normal z-scale and is therefore not a probability. In fact, we observed that the empirical 5% quantile for the l * z ranged from -1.70 to -1.58, thus around the nominal threshold Φ -1 (.05) = -1.64, the 5% quantile of the standard normal distribution. On the probability scale, these quantiles correspond to Φ(-1.70) = .045 to Φ(-1.58) = .057. This result confirms that the asymptotic standard normal approximation proposed by Snijders (2001) works well even at the shortest test length considered here (I = 12). Figure 2 shows that the thresholds for ppp S were close to the nominal 5% (between 5.0% and 5.8%), whereas those for ppp SM were slightly larger (between 6.0% and 6.7%). Thus, ppp S requires little to no threshold correction and ppp SM requires a small correction, at least under the conditions that we simulated. The situation is different for the remaining ppp approaches. The 5% calibrated thresholds for ppp GM (ranging between 11.3% and 12.4%) and ppp RB (between 11.2% and 13.1%) are clearly larger than the nominal 5% and were also considerably more variable across replications.

This result confirms that relying on the nominal 5% threshold can lead to an overly conservative assessment, resulting in reduced power. We used these empirically derived critical thresholds for all PFSs (including l * z and ppp S , for which they are close to the nominal ones) to flag misfitting response patterns in the power studies. This ensures that all PFSs are comparable at the same Type I error rate, which would not be the case with nominal thresholds (see Figure 1). Under the null model of no misfit one might expect a mean ppp of .50, but this need not hold. In fact, ppp values are in general not uniformly distributed under the null model, even asymptotically (Bayarri & Berger, 2000; Robins et al., 2000). Our results show that the mean ppp ranged between .42 and .55 across approaches and test lengths, and in some cases clearly deviated from .50 (see Figure S3 in the supplementary material). Our general advice is to always calibrate the thresholds to be used in aberrant response pattern detection. Using a simulation scheme under the null model of no misfit, as done in this simulation, is one simple means to do this.

Another question of interest is whether a calibrated threshold for a PFS works equally well across the entire θ ability range. This is important because in practice we typically rely on one threshold for classifying all response patterns in a data set as either aberrant or not aberrant. Figure 3 shows the Type I error rate by ability bin at the calibrated 5% thresholds. By construction, the Type I error rates average to about 5% across bins. l * z and ppp S were stable across the θ range for I ≥ 30, and somewhat less so for I = 12 and extreme θ values. We infer that, at least for scales that are not too short, the use of calibrated thresholds across θ levels is justified for these two PFSs. ppp SM was liberal near θ = 0 and conservative at the extremes. ppp GM and ppp RB showed the strongest dependence on ability. These PFSs flagged over 10% of persons near θ = 0 but at most 2.8% at |θ| ≥ 2. Results for critical levels of 1%, 2%, and 10% were analogous (Figure S4 in the supplementary material). Marginal calibration of thresholds for classification is therefore questionable for ppp GM and ppp RB.

In sum, at the nominal 5% threshold, ppp S was the PFS with empirical Type I error rates closest to the nominal level. ppp SM was slightly conservative, and ppp GM and ppp RB were very conservative. These results strongly suggest that, in general, the best course of action is to calibrate the critical values to use for flagging aberrant response patterns, in particular for ppp GM and ppp RB . Furthermore, at the calibrated thresholds, ppp S was the most stable ppp-based PFS across ability. For ppp GM and ppp RB , a single calibrated threshold across ability levels is questionable because it seems to strongly depend on θ. Simulation Study 2: Power Lack of motivation Figure 4 displays the detection rates under lack of motivation for all PFSs as a function of the proportion of aberrant items (PropAbIt), for each test length I. Detection rates ranged from about 51% (I = 12, PropAbIt = 1/6) to 83% (I = 60, PropAbIt = 1/2), and increased with both I and PropAbIt. The ppp S and ppp SM statistics consistently showed the highest detection rates, comparable to the frequentist l * z . The detection rates for ppp GM and ppp RB were lower in comparison, and the difference increased with both I and PropAbIt. Results at other critical levels were analogous (Figure S5 in the supplementary material). Item disclosure Figure 5 displays the detection rates under item disclosure. Detection rates ranged from about 54% (I = 12, PropAbIt = 1/2) to 83% (I = 60, PropAbIt = 1/6), and increased with I. In contrast to lack of motivation, detection rates mostly decreased as PropAbIt increased. This finding may be the result of a higher proportion of correct answers to the most difficult items leading to an overestimation of the ability parameters.

This overestimation therefore reduced the apparent discrepancy between the observed inflated item scores and the model-predicted response patterns. The ppp S statistic was the most powerful ppp-based statistic and performed similarly to l * z . The ppp SM statistic was less powerful, and the difference increased with both I and PropAbIt. The ppp GM and the ppp RB statistics performed similarly to each other and clearly worse than ppp S and ppp SM.

Results at other critical levels were analogous (Figure S6 in the supplementary material). Detection rates at the calibrated 5% thresholds for the item disclosure response behavior, as a function of the proportion of aberrant items, for each test length, averaged over abilities uniformly distributed on [-3, 3].

Speeding

powerful, followed by ppp SM ; ppp S and l * z performed the worst. Results varied somewhat according to the critical level (Figure S7 in the supplementary material): at the 1% and 2% levels ppp GM and ppp RB were less powerful than l * z , whereas at the 10% level they were more powerful, for I ≥ 30. Thus, unlike the other misfit types, no ppp approach consistently outperformed the others. This example underlines the importance of trying out a variety of person-fit checks, as there is seemingly no person-fit approach that is more powerful across the board. As can be seen in Figure 7, the power to detect lack of motivation increased strongly with θ, being close to 100% for θ ≥ 1 except when I = 12 and PropAbIt = 1/6.

Power as a function of θ

For large θ the lack of motivation behavior is extremely strong (the probability of a correct response to the easiest items drops from nearly 1 to .2). The net effect is that even conservative PFSs such as ppp GM and ppp RB are able to detect lack of motivation for large θ, despite being expected to underperform at these θ levels (see Figure 3). For lower ability levels ppp GM and ppp RB tend to perform worse, especially when I ≥ 30.

Empirical example

To showcase how the ppp-based approaches can be applied in practice, we ran a full analysis using the openly available SAT12 data set from the mirt R package (Chalmers, 2012) (all analysis files are available at https://osf.io/rsfv7/overview?view_only=0eda2c21f6f2476db10cb128188c23cc). The SAT12 data set consists of the responses of N = 600 examinees to I = 32 multiple-choice items of a grade-12 science test, scored as correct (1) or incorrect (0). Since we did not have item parameter estimates available, we fitted a Bayesian 2PL model in Stan (Stan

Detection rates at the calibrated 5% thresholds for the lack of motivation response behavior, as a function of the latent ability θ, for each test length and level of PropAbIt.

Development Team, 2026) through the cmdstanr interface (Gabry et al., 2025). We fitted four chains, each with 1000 warm-up and 1000 sampling iterations. We used the following priors: α i ∼ Lognormal(0, 0.5), β i ∼ N (0, 1) and θ n ∼ N (0, 1), for i = 1, . . . , I and n = 1, . . . , N . We ran some convergence checks after fitting the model; no issues were detected. The posterior medians of α i and β i were taken as the known item parameters.

We then conducted the person-fit analyses, following the same steps as in the simulation studies. First, in the calibration step, we calibrated the 5% thresholds as in the Type I Error simulation study: we generated 20 replications of 1000 model-fitting response vectors from the estimated item parameters (here with θ ∼ N (0, 1), the population assumed by the model) and then averaged the 5% quantiles of each PFS across the replications. The calibrated thresholds were -1.695, .066, .047, .068, and .049 for the l * z , ppp GM , ppp S , ppp RB , and ppp SM PFSs, respectively. As in the simulations, the thresholds for ppp GM and ppp RB were clearly above the nominal .05 value. Second, in the implementation step, we computed all five PFSs for every examinee (S = 250 posterior draws per examinee) and flagged those below the calibrated thresholds.

The l * z , ppp GM , ppp S , ppp RB , and ppp SM PFSs flagged 7.0%, 6.5%, 7.2%, 6.5%, and 7.0% of the examinees, respectively. Agreement among the PFSs was high: 549 examinees (91.5%) were flagged by none of them, 29 (4.8%) by all five, and 22 (3.7%) by some but not all. In particular, over half of the flagged examinees were identified by all the PFSs considered. Figure 8 displays the so-called person response function (PRF; Sijtsma and Meijer, 2001) of four selected examinees. The PRF defines the probability of a correct response as a function of item difficulty. For response vectors that fit the IRT model, the PRF is expected to be monotonically decreasing (thus, the more difficult an item is, the lower the probability of answering it correctly). Each panel in Figure 8 displays two lines.

The solid black line corresponds to data-implied probabilities of a correct response smoothed over item difficulty; similarly, the examinee's model-implied probabilities of a correct response are plotted in dashed red.

Examinee #502 (top-left panel) was not flagged by any PFS. It can be seen that the probability of a correct response decreases with item difficulty, as expected by the model.

Examinee #279 (top-right), on the other hand, was flagged by all PFSs. This response pattern is flagged because the examinee missed an unexpectedly large number of relatively easy items (-1.5 < b i < -0.5), combined with an unexpected success on harder items (0 < b i < 1). Examinee #438 (bottom-left) was flagged by all ppp statistics but not by l * z.

This examinee provided incorrect answers to many items with difficulty above -2, but two small clusters of items (with difficulties between -1.5 and -0.5, and between 1.5 and 2.5) were correctly answered. As a consequence, the PRF for this examinee displays two local increases that were detected by the ppp-based PFSs. Examinee #475 (bottom-right) was flagged by l * z but not by any ppp statistic. This examinee performed extremely well across all items, in particular items of low to intermediate difficulty. Because of this, the existence of two missed easy items (both with difficulty below -1) was flagged as suspect by l * z only.

The last two examinees illustrate that the PFSs may disagree about borderline patterns. It is therefore always advisable to combine several person-fit checks.

Discussion

Person-fit analyses in the IRT framework are important to check the validity of the responses provided by each subject. The Bayesian paradigm is appealing in this regard, because it directly accommodates the uncertainty of the model parameters in the inference.

Through the posterior predictive distribution it is possible to contrast an observed response pattern with corresponding model-fitting response patterns. Large deviations between the two types of responses should be interpreted as a signal warranting further investigation.

While this Bayesian approach in person-fit analysis is not novel, some of the implementations that we explored in our analyses are new. Of the four Bayesian PFSs that we considered, two (ppp GM and ppp S ) were previously proposed and two (ppp RB and ppp SM ) were new. The new proposals were based on earlier work on PPCs by Berkhof et al. (2004) and had not previously been evaluated in person-fit research.

We assessed through two simulation studies how the ppp PFSs performed under two generic situations: Absence and presence of person misfit. The Type I Error simulation study was set under the null model of no person misfit, allowing us to check whether the empirical Type I error rates were close to the nominal 5% rate. It was found that, at the nominal 5% threshold, ppp S was the best calibrated ppp approach, with empirical Type I error rates closely matching the nominal level, and that ppp SM was slightly conservative. In contrast, ppp GM and ppp RB were conservative (too low Type I error rates, possibly leading to unacceptably low detection power rates). Thus, especially for ppp GM and ppp RB , empirical threshold calibration is strongly recommended. Ultimately, we think that estimating thresholds that are tailored to the data, model, and test in hand is often a better approach than relying on nominal thresholds derived from asymptotic distributions.

The power studies compared the performance of the ppp PFSs under three different types of aberrant response behavior (lack of motivation, item disclosure, and speeding).

For lack of motivation and item disclosure, ppp S and ppp SM consistently outperformed ppp GM and ppp RB . The good performance of ppp S is consistent with the view that PPC-based person-fit checks work well when the mean of the discrepancy does not depend on θ (Robins et al., 2000; Sinharay, 2015a). However, the dependence of ppp The power studies underlined the importance of test length in person-fit analyses.

Across all misfit types and approaches, the test length I had a large effect on detection rates. Short tests (represented by the I = 12 condition in our simulations) yielded dramatically lower power. This finding was consistent across all the ppp statistics that we tested. Moreover, this result is not restricted to the Bayesian ppp PFS, as also the classical l * z suffered from the same limitation. For practitioners, it is important to include enough items to have sufficient power for detecting aberrant response behaviors. In general, person-fit analysis is most appropriate for tests of moderate to long length.

The power studies also highlighted a known limitation of person-fit analysis (e.g., St-Onge et al., 2011): When the proportion of aberrant item scores is too large, person-fit analyses tend to lose sensitivity. Simply put, in such cases we can say that aberrant becomes the new normal. Model parameter estimates such as the ability parameter θ may be over-or underestimated, and calibrated thresholds may also be biased. In our simulations this occurred under item disclosure, where ppp GM , ppp RB , and ppp SM were more affected than ppp S and the classical l * z . The main message for practitioners is that they should not expect a person-fit analysis to just 'sort it all out'. More effort in good test construction and data collection can help a lot to mitigate this type of problem.

Limitations and future research

Several limitations of the present study suggest directions for future research. First, our simulations assumed that item parameters were known through prior calibration.

While this is a realistic assumption in some situations, practitioners may also need to perform item parameter estimation when analyzing their data. The Bayesian PPC approach advocated in this paper extends naturally to this situation. Incorporating full item parameter uncertainty within the Bayesian framework is possible by allowing the full posterior of ω, encompassing both person and item parameters, to take part in the computation of the ppp-based PFSs. We conducted some preliminary explorations of this case. While it is technically simple to implement, it is computationally expensive. The grid approximation algorithm that we used to sample from p(θ|y) must be replaced by a more elaborate MCMC sampling scheme (for example, based on Stan or JAGS).

Such MCMC algorithms take time to run, especially if executed many thousands of times through simulation studies. More work to develop efficient simulations in this important practical situation is therefore needed. A related limitation concerns what could happen in case of model misfit. An IRT model might fail to accurately describe the observed data for various reasons (e.g., because the sample included too many examinees exhibiting aberrant response behavior, because the assumed dimensionality is incorrect, or because local independence is violated). In such cases, model misfit can propagate into the threshold calibration step. It may also directly undermine the reliability of the person-fit flagging detection stage (i.e., the comparison of each PFS to its threshold). Addressing this issue is an important direction for future research, for both the Bayesian ppp approaches and classical statistics.

Another limitation is the fact that some PFSs do not perform well based on a single critical threshold calibrated across the entire ability range. This was the case for ppp GM and ppp RB in our analyses, as shown in Figure 7 and especially in Figure 3. There are alternative approaches that tailor the calibration to each data set. For example, Van Kollenburg et al. (2017) compare the observed ppp to a reference distribution of ppp values computed on data sets simulated from the posterior distribution, which yields a calibrated p-value. In our setting, this would amount to doing this for each examinee, which would increase the computational cost. Their approach was developed with vague, data-dominated priors, whereas our analyses used a standard normal prior for each examinee. It is unclear whether this approach would remove the dependence on θ observed for ppp GM and ppp RB . Calibrating thresholds conditional on an estimate of θ is another possibility that we did not explore in the simulations. More generally, both the ppp values (through the prior on θ) and the calibrated thresholds (through the reference distribution of θ) depend on distributional assumptions about θ. Future research that focuses on the sensitivity of these procedures to sensible choices of prior distributions would be helpful.

Finally, the aberrant behaviors were operationalized following previous simulation studies (De La Torre & Deng, 2008; Glas & Meijer, 2003; Sinharay, 2015a): guessing on the easiest items (lack of motivation), pre-knowledge of the hardest items (item disclosure), and guessing on the hardest items (speeding). This decision allows comparison with earlier results, but it must be recognized that it is only one of many ways to operationalize these behaviors. Different operationalizations may lead to different power results, and the relative performance of the PFSs may differ accordingly.

The present study was restricted to one particular IRT model (the 2PL for dichotomous items) and one discrepancy measure (the l * z ). Extensions to other discrepancy measures, and also to other IRT models (say, dichotomous, polytomous, and possibly other types of IRT models such as multidimensional, multilevel, or trees) would broaden the applicability of the proposed approaches.

Berkhof et al. (2004, Section 4) focused on the discrepancy difference δ(y rep , y, θ) = T (y rep , θ) -T (y, θ). Under the null model of no misfit, both the observed data y and the replicated data y rep are assumed to have been generated from the same model. Any discrepancy between the two types of data should reflect only sampling variability, not model misfit. However, the posterior distribution of the model parameters θ typically only conditions on the observed data y. This creates a conceptual asymmetry: the posterior p(θ|y) is informed by the observed data y but not by the replicated data y rep . Berkhof and colleagues suggested that conditioning the posterior distribution of θ on both y and y rep could provide a better procedure. They further suggested averaging δ(y rep , y, θ) across this posterior distribution: ∆(y rep , y) = E δ(y rep , y, θ) y rep , y = δ(y rep , y, θ)p(θ|y rep , y) dθ. (10) Berkhof et al. (2004, p. 11) called it a "Rao-Blackwellized version of δ(y rep , y, θ)". By the Rao-Blackwell theorem (e.g., Casella and Berger, 2024, p. 277), ∆(y rep , y) has the same expected value as δ(y rep , y, θ) but variance no greater than that of δ(y rep , y, θ). This variance reduction has the potential to improve detection power. While attractive from a theoretical point of view, one practical difficulty of Equation 10 is the fact that it requires estimating a new posterior distribution p(θ|y rep , y) ppp SMBerkhof et al. The fact that ppp SM performed similarly to ppp S under lack of motivation is important since ppp SM is based on a fully Bayesian implementation of a PPC. Under speeding, no ppp approach consistently outperformed the others. More generally, no ppp approach was clearly more powerful than the classical l * z in any of the three power studies, except under speeding at I = 60. One advantage of the ppp-based approach is that it applies to any PFS, including those for which no null distribution is available (thus, beyond the l * z classical statistic). These outcomes are an important reminder of how important it is to use varying analytical strategies when performing any person-fit analysis. Since different PFSs may capitalize on different types of person misfit, a combination of person-fit checks can provide a more comprehensive assessment of response validity.
